name: Augmenting LLMs with Cases and Prompting Them to Perform CBR (Wilkerson & Leake; paper title: "On Implementing Case-Based Reasoning with Large Language Models")
venue: ICCBR 2024 -- 32nd International Conference on Case-Based Reasoning (Case-Based Reasoning Research and Development), Merida, Mexico, July 1-4, 2024. Published in Springer LNCS vol. 14775, pp. 404-417, DOI 10.1007/978-3-031-63646-2_26. The provided paper_url (homes.luddy.indiana.edu/.../p-24-02.pdf) is the authors' technical-report / preprint version of this peer-reviewed conference paper.
authors_affiliation: Kaitlynne Wilkerson and David Leake. Primary affiliation: Luddy School of Informatics, Computing, and Engineering, Indiana University, Bloomington, IN, USA ({kwilker, leake}@indiana.edu).
paper_url: https://homes.luddy.indiana.edu/leake/papers/p-24-02.pdf (tech-report version). Peer-reviewed version: https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-63646-2_26 (Springer LNCS 14775, pp. 404-417); DBLP: dblp.org/rec/conf/iccbr/WilkersonL24.
code_url: N/A (no official code repository is referenced in the paper; the case base was derived from a public Kaggle emergency-triage dataset, ChatGPT 3.5 prompts were entered by hand through the web interface, and Llama 2 70b-chat was run locally via llama.cpp / llama-cpp-python on IU's Big Red 200 supercomputer. No dedicated public repo was located.) [uncertain]
task_domain: Decision-making / classification (QA-style single-label prediction): medical triage classification -- assigning a Korean Triage and Acuity Scale (KTAS) level 1-5 to emergency-room patients from their vital signs and chief complaint. Framed as a case-based classification process implemented with LLMs.
problem_setting: Offline, single-agent, supervised classification with a small curated case base. Given a current patient's status (7 attribute-value features: sex, age, heart rate, respiratory rate, mental state, blood pressure, chief complaint), the LLM must output a KTAS triage number 1-5. A k-NN retrieval component first selects a small subset of prior labeled cases from a 102-case case base; that subset is injected into the LLM prompt. There is no model training/fine-tuning -- the study only varies prompting strategy (Direct Solution baseline vs Implicit-CBR vs Explicit-CBR) and the number/type of provided cases (1NN / 2NN / NUN). Interaction is one-shot per test case (ECBR uses a short multi-turn similarity-then-adapt prompt sequence). It is an empirical/exploratory study (the paper's stated purpose is to open the door to future investigation), testing whether LLMs benefit from being given cases and from being guided through CBR sub-processes (similarity assessment, adaptation, nearest-unlike-neighbor reasoning). 25 test cases (5 per class), 7 prompt/formulation types each = 175 prompts per LLM, run on ChatGPT 3.5 and Llama 2 70b-chat.
what_is_retrieved: cases -- prior labeled patient cases (problem-solution pairs: patient feature vector + expert-assigned KTAS triage number) drawn from the case base. The paper explicitly contrasts retrieving cases (concrete prior episodes aimed at the task) versus RAG-style text snippets of general facts.
retrieval_grounding: STATIC external corpus: retrieval targets a fixed, offline-constructed case base (102 cases sampled from a public Kaggle triage dataset). The case base is not written to or grown by the agent during deployment; it functions as a static external experience store (case base) rather than a growing/episodic memory.
completeness_vs_topk_objective: Fixed top-k retrieval objective: the k-NN component returns a fixed small set of nearest cases (k=1 for 1NN; k=2 for 2NN; NN + nearest-unlike-neighbor for NUN; for ECBR a fixed pool of 10 candidate cases is provided and the LLM is asked to select 1 or 2). The objective is a fixed-size top-k selection feeding a classification decision, not minimal-set completeness recovery or precision-driven variable-size recommendation.
cbr_cycle_coverage: [Retrieve, Reuse, Revise] -- Retrieve (k-NN nearest-neighbor case retrieval, and in ECBR the LLM additionally performs similarity assessment / case selection); Reuse + Revise (the LLM adapts/combines the retrieved case(s) -- the ICBR/ECBR adaptation step -- to produce a triage number for the new patient, i.e. reuse of the prior solution plus revision in light of similarities/differences). Retain is NOT implemented (no new cases are written back to the case base). So Retrieve=yes, Reuse=yes, Revise=yes, Retain=no.
explicit_cbr_grounding: True. The work explicitly frames itself as implementing Case-Based Reasoning with LLMs, cites Watson (CBR is a methodology not a technology), Leake, and the CBR literature on cases as explanations, and is published at ICCBR (the CBR conference). It explicitly invokes the CBR cycle phases (similarity assessment, adaptation) and CBR concepts (nearest neighbor, nearest unlike neighbor). It does not center on the Aamodt & Plaza four-R formalism in this preprint text but is unambiguously grounded in CBR.
retrieval_unit: case (problem-solution): a single prior patient case = attribute-value feature vector (sex, age, heart rate, respiratory rate, mental state, blood pressure, chief complaint) paired with its expert KTAS triage label. Retrieved as 1-2 full cases (ICBR) or selected from a 10-case candidate pool (ECBR).
index_source: Static corpus, offline-induced: the retrievable case base is a fixed set of 102 cases sampled once (random sample with >=1 case per class) from a public Kaggle emergency-triage dataset; missing-value instances were removed. Not online/test-time-induced and not hybrid.
index_structure_topology: Flat case base queried by a weighted-Euclidean-distance k-NN over the 7 attribute features (categorical distance 1/0; textual chief-complaint compared by semantic similarity via sentence-transformer all-mpnet-base-v2 + cosine). No graph, hierarchy, or cluster structure; a flat metric-space index with per-feature weights tuned by hill climbing.
retriever_type: Hybrid/classical: a weighted-Euclidean k-NN retriever (numeric/categorical features) augmented with dense semantic similarity (all-mpnet-base-v2 sentence embeddings + PyTorch cosine similarity) for the textual chief-complaint feature. In the ECBR condition, the LLM itself acts as a second-stage retriever/selector (LLM-as-retriever for similarity assessment) over a 10-case pool provided by k-NN.
retriever_learning_signal: Mostly none (off-the-shelf) plus a lightweight weight-tuning step: the k-NN feature weights were selected by hill climbing to maximize k-NN training accuracy (best weighted-1-NN accuracy 48%; final weights Respiratory Rate=1.0, Mental State=0.25, Chief Complaint=0.25, all others=0.001). The sentence-transformer (all-mpnet-base-v2) is used off-the-shelf. The LLMs are not trained/fine-tuned for retrieval; LLM similarity assessment is pure zero-shot prompting (no learning signal).
query_construction: Raw current-patient status in textual attribute-value form (e.g. 'Patient Status: Sex: Female, Age: 50, Chief complaint: ..., Mental state: Pain Response, Heart Rate: 37, Respirations: 28, Blood Pressure: 50/33'). The same patient description serves as the k-NN query and as the LLM prompt context. No query decomposition, expansion, or intent extraction.
query_granularity: Task-level (one-shot at t=0): a single query per test case (the whole patient description), used once to retrieve cases before the LLM produces a classification. No per-step or trajectory-level re-querying.
when_to_retrieve: One-shot: cases are retrieved once per test case (via k-NN) before prompting the LLM. In the ECBR condition there is a fixed, scripted two-stage prompt (first similarity assessment to select case(s) from the provided pool, then adaptation), but retrieval is not iterative/active/uncertainty-triggered.
retrieval_trigger_signal: Fixed schedule: retrieval is always performed once per incoming test case (k-NN selects the case subset). For ECBR, the similarity-assessment selection step is likewise always performed on a fixed schedule, not gated by confidence/uncertainty or a learned router.
reranking: None as a dedicated module. The k-NN ordering by weighted distance provides the nearest neighbor(s); for ECBR the LLM re-selects/reorders by picking the most-similar case(s) from the 10-case pool (an LLM-as-selector step that loosely acts as reranking), but there is no cross-encoder/RRF/instruction-tuned reranker.
retrieved_context_refinement: None: retrieved cases are passed verbatim (as attribute-value text) into the prompt with no decomposition, distillation, compression, or distractor filtering. The only post-hoc processing is a manual hallucination check on the LLM output (responses where the LLM hallucinated case information were discarded and re-run), which is a sanity check on output rather than refinement of retrieved context.
tool_document_engineering: N/A (no tools/APIs; retrieved units are patient cases, not tool documents).
index_content_separation: N/A -- cases are small attribute-value records stored and loaded together; no lightweight-index-then-heavy-content progressive-disclosure separation.
dynamic_index_and_protocol: N/A (no tool index or external API protocol; the case base is a static local store).
how_retrieved_used: Prompt augmentation + case adaptation: retrieved prior case(s) are concatenated into the LLM prompt, and the LLM is instructed to use the similarities and differences between the current patient and the prior case(s) to assign a triage number -- i.e. the LLM performs case reuse/adaptation in natural language. In ICBR the adaptation is implicit (LLM given the case and asked to solve); in ECBR the LLM is explicitly guided through similarity assessment (select case(s) from a pool) then adaptation. No training-signal or latent-token use.
planning_integration: Retrieve-then-solve with one-shot exemplar(s) at decision time: k-NN retrieves case(s), which are injected as prompt context, and the LLM produces a single classification (the 'solution'). For ECBR there is a short fixed plan-like sequence (similarity-assessment prompt -> adaptation prompt). There is no tree search, MCTS, hierarchical subtask decomposition, or per-step interleaving -- this is a single classification decision, not multi-step planning.
reasoning_search_interleaving_granularit: Per-answer (per-case): one retrieval and (for ICBR) one conditioned generation produce one triage label per test case. ECBR uses two scripted turns (similarity assessment then adaptation) but retrieval is not interwoven per CoT-step or per token.
adaptation_mechanism: LLM-prompted adaptation: the retrieved case's solution (a prior patient's KTAS number) is adapted by prompting the LLM to weigh similarities and differences between the current patient and the prior case(s) and to assign a (possibly different) triage number. The paper operationally defines 'adaptation occurred' as the LLM output differing from the retrieved nearest neighbor's label, and measures adaptation rates per model (e.g. ChatGPT adapted >50% of the time across most prompts; Llama 2 adapted much less often). For NUN formulations a counterfactual (nearest-unlike-neighbor) is provided to help delineate class boundaries during adaptation. No execution-feedback, critic, or RL-based revision.
retrieved_item_representation: Raw case in attribute-value text form: the prior patient's feature values plus its triage label, presented verbatim as structured text in the prompt (e.g. 'Sex: ..., Age: ..., Heart Rate: ..., ... ,' with the KTAS number). No distillation to a strategy/guideline, no program/skill, no latent tokens.
abstraction_level_of_retrieved_unit: Single demonstration / concrete prior case (problem-solution pair): a literal prior solved patient case, not a distilled strategy, abstracted rule, or reusable workflow. The NUN formulation additionally supplies a counterfactual concrete case.
noise_robustness_mechanism: Limited / largely manual: (1) a post-generation hallucination sanity check -- because the original case is available, responses in which the LLM hallucinated case attributes were detected and discarded/re-run (the paper highlights this case-grounded sanity check as a robustness benefit of CBR over plain generation); (2) providing multiple cases (2NN) and a counterfactual (NUN) is motivated as increasing robustness of the response. No retriever-aware training, learned relevance evaluator, reason-in-documents refinement, or distractor-aware SFT.
memory_type: none (static case base) -- the retrievable store is a fixed external case base used at inference; it is not an agent-written episodic memory, skill-library, workflow, graph, or latent memory. (Closest descriptor: a static case base, i.e. an external experience corpus that is read-only at test time.)
write_back: False -- the system does not store new experiences/cases/solutions back into the case base; the 102-case case base is fixed and read-only during the experiment. (Retain phase of the CBR cycle is not implemented.)
online_growth: No -- the case base does not grow during deployment/test-time; it is frozen after the offline sampling step.
write_back_trigger: Never -- no write-back mechanism exists; nothing is written to the case base on success, on failure, per-step, reflectively, or via human validation.
failure_experience_usage: Success-only cases (positive labeled cases) are stored/retrieved; failed or negative LLM trajectories are not stored or reused. The NUN (nearest-unlike-neighbor / counterfactual) formulation does inject a contrasting case of a DIFFERENT class to help delineate decision boundaries, but this is a correctly-labeled contrastive case from the static case base, not a stored failure experience.
memory_evolution_update: N/A -- the case base is static (read-only); stored entries are never mutated, merged, delta-updated, refined, or pruned during the experiment (other than the one-time offline removal of missing-value instances and sampling to 102 cases).
retrieval_as_learned_policy: No -- case selection is fixed: weighted k-NN nearest-neighbor retrieval (weights set once by hill climbing). In ECBR the LLM selects cases via zero-shot prompting, which is not a trained/RL retrieval policy. No M-MDP / soft Q-learning / RL retrieval.
cross_agent_or_cross_framework_sharing: No -- single-agent, single-model use of a private static case base; no memory/experience sharing across multiple agents or frameworks. (Two LLMs, ChatGPT and Llama 2, are compared but each is run independently on the same case base, not sharing experience.)
benchmarks: A custom medical-triage classification testbed built from a public Kaggle emergency-service triage dataset (originally 1,267 patients, 24 vital signs/assessments, KTAS labels 1-5 assigned by 3 triage experts). The authors narrowed to 7 features, removed missing-value instances, used a 102-case case base and a 25-case test set (5 per class). No standard public benchmark suite; LLMs tested: ChatGPT 3.5 and Llama 2 70b-chat.
benchmark_family: decision-making / single-label classification (medical triage). Not part of standard QA / web / embodied / tool / code / memory / decision-RL benchmark families; it is a custom small-scale classification testbed.
baselines: (1) Unweighted 1-NN classifier (full 102-case case base); (2) Weighted 1-NN classifier (hill-climbing-optimized feature weights, full case base); (3) Direct Solution LLM prompt (no case provided) as the non-CBR LLM baseline, for each of ChatGPT and Llama 2. The CBR prompting conditions (ICBR / ECBR x 1NN/2NN/NUN) are compared against these.
key_metrics: Classification accuracy on the 25-case test set under three correctness criteria: Strict Accuracy (exact KTAS match); Correct-within-1-class-higher (accepting safe near-misses that over-triage); Correct-within-1-class-higher-or-lower. Secondary diagnostic metrics: similarity-assessment accuracy (rate at which the LLM-selected case matches the k-NN-selected case) and adaptation analysis (rate of adaptation, % of adapted cases that were correct, % of adaptations where the NN was already correct i.e. unnecessary adaptation).
headline_result: Providing cases improved LLM triage accuracy over the no-case Direct Solution baseline. The best prompt type overall was ICBR with the single nearest neighbor (ICBR 1NN): strict accuracy 60% with ChatGPT and 56% with Llama 2, versus the Direct Solution baseline of 28% for both LLMs, and outperforming the optimized weighted-1-NN classifier (48%) and unweighted 1-NN (28%) for both models.
ablations: The study is structured as a set of controlled comparisons (effectively ablations) over prompt type and case formulation: (1) Direct Solution (no case) vs ICBR vs ECBR -- ICBR/ECBR generally match or beat the no-case baseline, showing cases provide useful knowledge. (2) Number/type of cases: 1NN vs 2NN vs NUN -- ICBR 1NN best overall; a second similar case (2NN) helps in some settings (ICBR 2NN strong on Llama 2: 44% strict; ECBR 2NN strong on ChatGPT, e.g. 44% strict / 72% within-1-higher); the counterfactual NUN formulation generally did not help and ECBR NUN was the weakest (28% strict on both LLMs). (3) Implicit vs Explicit CBR: ICBR (k-NN-selected case) >= ECBR (LLM-selected case), attributed to poor LLM similarity assessment. (4) Similarity-assessment diagnostic (Table 3): LLM-vs-k-NN agreement was low for both models (e.g. ECBR 1NN: ChatGPT 20%, Llama 2 28%; ECBR 2NN second-case: ChatGPT 4%, Llama 2 16%), with Llama 2 slightly better at selecting 2NN/NUN. (5) Adaptation diagnostic (Table 4): ChatGPT adapts much more often than Llama 2 (ICBR 1NN adaptation rate 56% vs 64%; ECBR 2NN 84% vs 32%); Llama 2's lower and less-correct adaptation likely explains its weaker ECBR 2NN results. Conclusion: adaptation ability is LLM-specific and drives which prompt/case formulation is best.
evaluation_decoupling: Partially yes: the LLM's intrinsic similarity-assessment quality (agreement with k-NN-chosen cases, Table 3) and its adaptation behavior (Table 4) are reported separately from end-to-end triage accuracy (Table 2). However these are diagnostic process metrics, not standard IR metrics (no Recall@k / nDCG); the k-NN retriever's own retrieval quality is not separately scored beyond k-NN classification accuracy.
process_vs_outcome_metrics: Both: the primary metric is the outcome (triage classification accuracy under three criteria), but the paper also reports intermediate process quality -- similarity-assessment correctness (does the LLM pick the same case as k-NN) and adaptation analysis (how often adaptation occurs, whether it is correct, whether it was unnecessary). These process metrics are used to explain the outcome differences between ChatGPT and Llama 2.
cost_efficiency_tradeoff: Not quantified in terms of latency/API cost/tokens. The study is small-scale (25 test cases x 7 prompt types = 175 prompts per LLM); ChatGPT prompts were entered by hand via the web interface over a single day (noted as not parameter-controllable and not replicable), while Llama 2 70b-chat was run locally (temperature 0, top_p 0.9) on IU's Big Red 200 supercomputer for replicability. The motivation includes a knowledge-acquisition-cost argument: using LLM knowledge to bypass costly manual CBR knowledge engineering in knowledge-rich domains. No explicit cost/accuracy tradeoff numbers.
context_budget_and_selection_count: Fixed-k, small budget driven by prompt-size limits: the authors explicitly note prompt-size limitations prevented presenting the whole case base, so an initial k-NN retrieval selects a small subset. ICBR injects 1 case (1NN) or 2 cases (2NN/NUN). ECBR presents a fixed pool of 10 candidate cases and asks the LLM to select 1 (1NN) or 2 (2NN / NN+NUN). k is fixed per formulation (not adaptive/precision-driven). Llama 2 generation used temperature 0, top_p 0.9.
benchmark_construction_and_size: Custom testbed (not a released benchmark): source = public Kaggle emergency-service triage dataset (1,267 patients, 24 features, KTAS 1-5 expert labels). Construction: narrowed to 7 commonly-used triage features (sex, age, heart rate, respiratory rate, mental state, blood pressure, chief complaint), removed missing-value instances, randomly sampled a 102-case case base (>=1 per class) and a 25-case test set (5 per class). Answer verifiability: KTAS labels assigned by three triage experts in the original dataset serve as ground truth. Difficulty signal: triage is noisy/subjective; best baseline (weighted 1-NN) reaches only 48% strict accuracy and the best LLM condition (ICBR 1NN, ChatGPT) reaches 60% strict accuracy.
builds_on: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for LLMs (Lewis et al. 2020; Gao et al. survey 2023); generated/external-knowledge prompting for commonsense reasoning (Liu et al. 2021); classical CBR as a methodology not a technology (Watson 1996) and CBR knowledge/explanation work (Leake; Cheetham & Watson 2005; Cunningham et al. 2003; Gates, Leake & Wilkerson 2023 'Cases are King' user study); CBR-RAG for legal QA (Wiratunga et al. 2024) as the prior example of giving LLMs cases. Uses Llama 2 (Touvron et al. 2023), ChatGPT 3.5, sentence-transformers all-mpnet-base-v2, llama.cpp / llama-cpp-python.
contrasts_with: Standard RAG (text-snippet retrieval): the paper explicitly contrasts providing LLMs with cases (concrete prior episodes aimed at the task, prompting CBR sub-processes) against RAG, which retrieves general fact snippets and merely adds context. It also contrasts implicit case use (ICBR) vs explicitly guiding the LLM through CBR steps (ECBR / similarity assessment + adaptation), and contrasts LLM similarity assessment against k-NN similarity, and CBR-augmented prompting against a knowledge-light k-NN classifier and a no-case Direct Solution LLM baseline.
lineage: Group D (case-based planning / case-based reasoning with LLMs). An exploratory ICCBR-2024 study positioned at the intersection of CBR and LLMs: it advances the case-augmented-generation lineage (cases instead of RAG snippets) and specifically probes whether prompting LLMs through CBR sub-processes (similarity assessment, adaptation, nearest-unlike-neighbor) helps. Sits alongside CBR-RAG (Wiratunga et al. 2024) and feeds the authors' subsequent CBR-LLM reliability / hallucination-feedback work (CBR-LLM workshop papers, CEUR Vol-3708, Vol-3993).
